title: Microsoft vs. Salesforce: One Software Stock Remains a Top Pick, the Other Has Something to Prove, Says RBC
detail:

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) sell to many of the same corporate customers, and both are betting that AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on its own, will become a major source of revenue.

Today, Microsoft got an uncomfortable reminder of how much those customers rely on it. A global outage that started Thursday afternoon knocked Outlook and parts of Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services offline for millions of users, and it dragged into Friday after the first fixes didn't hold. Microsoft says it has found no sign of malicious activity.

Microsoft shares are down around 1.5% in premarket trading on Friday. Salesforce has had a tough year of its own, with the stock down about 18% year to date.

RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria covers both tech giants and published notes on each this week, ahead of Microsoft's Ignite conference (November 17-20) and Salesforce's fiscal third-quarter report on December 2.

Microsoft

Starting with Microsoft, the analyst expects Ignite to show how far the company has pushed AI into every layer of its business, from data centers and in-house chips to apps and security. However, he doesn't see the event moving the stock much in the short term.

The backdrop is strong. Azure grew 48% in constant currency last quarter, up from 43% the quarter before, and management has guided for 49% to 50% this quarter. Jaluria believes demand still outruns the capacity Microsoft can bring online, which makes that guidance look cautious, though the year-ago comparison is a tough one. He wants updates on capacity and on Maia 300, the custom chip unveiled in October, which Microsoft is designing to be 40% more efficient than leading GPU setups and expects to roll out at multi-gigawatt scale in 2027.

Then there's Copilot. Daily users jumped about 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold year over year, while customers with over 50,000 Microsoft 365 seats grew more than 8x. Jaluria thinks investors are overlooking Microsoft's shift toward usage-based pricing, which Cowork and GitHub Copilot already use. Charging for consumption rather than per user could lift the ceiling on what Microsoft earns as agents take on more work, and he expects Ignite to add new agent-building and management tools.

title: Microsoft Outage Disrupts Oil Trader Data and Dealmaking

(Bloomberg) -- Around noon on Thursday, Oklahoma-based commodities trader Dennis Kissler's inbox went eerily quiet, even as new comments on the Iran war by US President Donald Trump sent oil into a volatile stretch.

It took another hour for his team to realize emails weren't going through and start calling clients instead.

"We were in a one hour black hole. It definitely threw us off," said Kissler, who uses Microsoft Corp.'s Outlook to communicate with clients, many of whom are executives at shale producers.

A major outage of Microsoft's flagship software starting Thursday hit government offices, businesses and traders around the world, leaving many, like Kissler, who serves as senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc., to try other forms of communication. In some cases, traders reverted to old-school methods, including employees taking orders and relaying fills by phone and fax machine.

For oil traders, the outage added another layer of complexity to a market already upended by months of conflict in the Middle East. Any delay to putting on or unwinding a trade can prove costly in today's headline-driven market, where prices can turn on a dime as traders parse every development tied to US-Iran peace talks.

Microsoft on Friday said it was making progress in efforts to restore access and service availability. Still, the company warned that users of more than 20 products and services may continue to encounter errors.

One of the key pain points for traders during the outage has been commodity price data.

In Iowa, refined products broker Ken Malloy realized just before noon local time on Thursday that he couldn't access his email. He tried for hours but ultimately couldn't send out a report detailing fuel prices for clients of Kembro Fuel Brokers that he publishes four times a day. He continued to try late into the night but the issue wasn't fixed and he ended up sending Thursday's report early Friday morning.

Commodity traders and the oil and gas industry more broadly — from drillers to refiners — rely on prices published by several reporting agencies. One of the main agencies, S&P Global's division Platts, alerted clients Thursday that price updates may be delayed due to the outage and asked market participants who share information with them to communicate via phone or instant messenger as the company was unable to receive data via email.

title: AMD Stock Looks Poised to Revisit Its All-Time Highs

Advanced Micro Devices' (AMD) stock looks poised to revisit its all-time highs. The market has already bought into its growth story. Now, the next opportunity may lie in how much of that growth turns into profits. After a triple-digit gain in 2026, the stock has pulled back from its October record highs, but the fundamentals help explain much of that rally.

In its third-quarter earnings report, released on November 3, the Santa Clara, California-based chipmaker reported that its Data Center revenue nearly doubled, along with a great improvement in margins.

The most interesting part may still be ahead. With much greater visibility into 2027, I believe the market still underestimates the company's earnings growth potential. That's why I remain bullish, even with an already demanding valuation.

AMD's Data Center Growth Explains Much of the Rally

First, I think it's important to put AMD's remarkable triple-digit rally this year into context. I see two key metrics that have marked a turning point in the company's investment thesis: Data Center revenue growth and forward revenue growth.

Let's start by breaking down the first metric. Basically, the market has gone from viewing AMD as a central processing unit (CPU) manufacturer trying to gain ground in artificial intelligence (AI) graphics processing units (GPUs) to treating it as a potential second major AI infrastructure platform, behind Nvidia (NVDA).

The acceleration driven by AI demand really began to show up in AMD's results in 2026, something that wasn't nearly as pronounced in 2025. To be more specific, in the third quarter of 2025, AMD generated $4.34 billion in Data Center revenue, up 22% year-over-year. A year later, that revenue reached $8.55 billion, a 97% jump, driven by both EPYC processors, benefiting particularly from the growth of AI agents, and Instinct MI450 GPUs. As a result, Data Center now accounts for 64% of the company's total revenue, compared to less than 50% in the same period last year.

As if that weren't enough, this growth came with a considerable improvement in the segment's profitability. Data Center's operating margin rose from 25% to 34%. So, we're talking about a company whose core business has nearly doubled in size while its margins have expanded by an impressive 9 percentage points.
